title: Three Chords
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 36 of 40
content:
Danse learned three chords.

It took him two months.

Not because the chords were difficult.

Because every time he made a mistake, he tried to turn music practice into military discipline.

“Again,” he muttered.

The chord buzzed badly.

“Relax your hand.”

“I am relaxed.”

“You’re gripping the neck like it insulted Maxson.”

His fingers loosened.

“Again.”

“See? You do listen to me.”

“Occasionally.”

We sat on the porch of the rebuilt house. The borrowed guitar had become a permanent gift after the settlement musician found another instrument.

Danse had resisted accepting it.

Then spent six hours cleaning it.

Now he played the first chord.

Then the second.

Then the third.

All clean.

He stopped.

I grinned.

Danse looked at his fingers.

“Again.”

“No.”

“What?”

“You did it.”

“I can improve the transition speed.”

“Tomorrow.”

He frowned.

“I have momentum.”

“You have a successful ending. Learn to recognize one.”

That landed deeper than I intended.

Danse looked out over the road.

A caravan was moving in the distance. Sunlight warmed the dead grass. Somewhere behind the house, our new windmill squeaked every third rotation.

“I don’t know how,” he admitted.

“What?”

“Recognize an ending before something goes wrong.”

I sat beside him.

“You’re waiting for the next casualty.”

“Yes.”

“The next order.”

“Yes.”

“The next revelation that destroys your life.”

He gave me a look.

“Dramatic.”

“Accurate, though.”

His mouth twitched.

I touched the guitar.

“Three chords. Nothing went wrong.”

“Yet.”

“Danse.”

He exhaled.

“Three chords,” he said.

“Good.”

“Successful objective.”

“Not an objective.”

“Successful…”

He searched.

“Thing.”

I laughed.

“Perfect.”

He set the guitar aside.

Then pulled me into his lap with enough ease to remind me that civilian clothes had not changed how strong he was.

I made a surprised noise.

Danse looked pleased.

“That was deliberate.”

“I know.”

“Just clarifying.”

His arms settled around me.

We watched the sunset.

After a while I asked, “Do you miss the armor?”

“Yes.”

“Do you miss being a paladin?”

A longer pause.

“Yes.”

I waited.

“I don’t miss what I believed I had to be.”

I turned toward him.

“What was that?”

“Certain.”

The answer surprised me.

Danse looked down at his hands.

“I thought doubt was weakness. Commanders can’t hesitate. Soldiers can’t question every threat. You make decisions and live with them.”

“That part is still true.”

“Yes.”

“But?”

“But certainty became easier than thinking.”

That was the closest he had come to naming the thing that had almost killed him.

I kissed his cheek.

“Three chords.”

He smiled.

“Three chords.”

The next day he learned a fourth.

The fourth chord created a problem.

Three chords had been an experiment.

Four meant Danse now believed he should be able to play a song.

This was how I woke one morning to the same six seconds of music repeated from the porch with increasing hostility.

I pulled on a shirt and opened the door.

Danse sat in the early light with the guitar balanced on one knee, red scarf looped loosely around his neck because the morning was cold.

He played the progression.

Stopped.

Played it again.

Stopped.

“Are you fighting the song?” I asked.

“No.”

“You look like you’re fighting the song.”

“The transition is too slow.”

“It is six in the morning.”

“That is unrelated.”

“Nothing musical should happen at six in the morning unless somebody is being paid.”

Danse looked at me.

“You’re awake now.”

“Against my will.”

I sat beside him anyway.

He played again.

This time I recognized the shape of an old pre-War tune we had heard on a trader’s radio.

“You’ve been practicing in secret.”

“I practice while you’re doing supply runs.”

“Why?”

His fingers stopped.

The answer took long enough that I knew it mattered.

“I wanted to surprise you.”

That was almost offensively sweet.

I leaned my shoulder against his.

“You did.”

“It isn’t ready.”

“I didn’t say it was good.”

He looked wounded.

I laughed and kissed the corner of his jaw.

“It’s getting there.”

Danse stared at the strings.

“I don’t know why I care whether it sounds good to you.”

“Yes, you do.”

“Fine. I don’t know why I care this much.”

“That I believe.”

He set the guitar aside.

“When I was in the Brotherhood, praise was measurable. Accuracy scores. completed objectives. promotions. A superior told you whether you met the standard.”

“And now?”

“Now I play four chords on a porch and wait for your face to tell me whether it meant anything.”

I turned toward him.

“That sounds terrifying.”

“It is.”

“Good.”

His eyes narrowed.

“We have discussed your inappropriate use of that word.”

“I mean it’s vulnerable.”

“That does not make it good.”

“No. But you’re doing it anyway.”

He looked toward the road.

The windmill squeaked.

A crow landed on the fence and immediately reconsidered the location when Danse picked the guitar up again.

“This bird has better judgment than the dog,” I said.

“Quiet.”

He began the progression.

This time he did not stop when one chord buzzed.

He kept going.

The song remained imperfect. The rhythm dragged. One transition arrived late enough that I could practically see him wanting to restart.

He did not.

He reached the end.

Then looked at me.

I clapped once.

“Do not be patronizing.”

I clapped louder.

Danse tried not to smile.

Failed.

“You finished it,” I said.

“I made three errors.”

“And finished it.”

“The timing—”

“Finished.”

He breathed out.

“Yes.”

That afternoon the settlement held a small market. We brought repaired weapons, spare parts, and the guitar because one of the children had asked whether Danse would play.

He nearly refused.

Then looked at me.

I raised both hands.

“Your choice.”

He hated that answer.

He played anyway.

Ten people listened. Nobody cared about the late chord. A little girl danced in circles with Captain the dog until both fell over.

When Danse finished, the workshop owner cheered loudest.

He looked embarrassed.

Then happy.

Not proud because he had been best.

Proud because he had shared something unfinished and the world had not punished him for it.

The settlement asked him to play again the following week.

Danse assumed they were being polite.

“They heard the first performance,” he said. “They have sufficient information.”

“Maybe they liked it.”

“That would indicate poor judgment.”

He played anyway.

This time he made it through the first verse before missing the transition. His hand stopped automatically.

Nobody booed.

A child near the fire shouted, “Keep going!”

Danse looked at me.

I lifted both hands. “Not an order.”

He looked back at the strings.

Then continued from the next chord instead of restarting.

The mistake remained inside the song.

So did the song.

When he finished, the applause was louder than before.

Danse sat very still.

Later an old farmer came over and said, “My wife used to love that tune.”

“I played it badly,” Danse replied.

The farmer shrugged. “Still knew what it was.”

Danse had no answer.

On the porch afterward, he told me that sentence bothered him.

“Why?”

“Because I keep assuming imperfect means unrecognizable.”

I leaned against his shoulder.

“And?”

“And apparently that’s not always true.”

He played the troublesome transition once more.

It buzzed.

He did not start over.

After the applause, Danse packed the guitar as carefully as he once packed a laser rifle.

The old farmer stopped him again.

“Come by next week,” the man said. “I know another song you might like.”

Danse’s first instinct was visible: refuse before obligation could form.

Then he glanced at me.

Not for permission.

For orientation.

“I might,” he said.

The farmer nodded as if *might* were enough.

On the road, I bumped my shoulder against his.

“Look at you making social plans.”

“I made no commitment.”

“You said might.”

“That is explicitly noncommittal.”

“For you, that’s practically spontaneous.”

He muttered something about inaccurate standards.

But his hand found mine anyway.

Halfway down the road he played the troublesome transition while walking.

It was worse than before.

He laughed first.

Danse looked back once toward the fire, where someone else had started another song. He did not look embarrassed anymore. Mostly, he looked as though he wanted to remember the sound.

The strings had left shallow marks across his fingertips. He studied them with absurd satisfaction, like evidence that the afternoon had actually happened.

“Worth it?” I asked.

“Yes,” he said, and did not qualify the answer.

On the walk home, he carried the guitar over one shoulder.

“You know what the worst part is?” he asked.

“What?”

“I want to learn the whole song.”

I gasped theatrically.

“Ambition.”

“And another after that.”

“Dangerous.”

“I may even learn one you like.”

I took his free hand.

“I already like this one.”

“It was badly played.”

“That wasn’t what I said.”

Danse stopped.

He recognized the sentence.

One of his, from the beginning.

The smile came slowly.

“Fair point.”

We kept walking.

Behind us the settlement noise faded.

Ahead, our house waited with a porch large enough for two people, one guitar, and as many imperfect songs as he wanted to learn.

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
